title: "I'm Very Happy for It to Start Hallucinating a Little Bit": Using ClayFlect to Negotiate Multimodal AI Representations in Material Meaning-Making
summary: As AI enters reflection and emotional support, understanding how it can participate in personal meaning-making while preserving users' authority over interpretation is increasingly important. We present ClayFlect, a novel MLLM-powered system integrating tactile clay-making with conversational and visual generative AI, and report a mixed-methods study with 50 participants. Reflection developed across material, conversational, and generated forms rather than through AI interaction alone. Participants treated AI representations as provisional: they compared, redirected, reinterpreted, selectively incorporated, or left them aside as their artefacts and meanings evolved. Clay provided a directly manipulable space in which participants could continue developing meaning independently of the AI, while generated representations externalised possibilities beyond what they could readily make or visualise. We show how generative AI can participate through representations that remain negotiable, and derive implications for supporting movement across representations, preserving parallel sites of control, and allowing AI support to recede or deepen as reflection unfolds.

AI.tldr: ClayFlect is a mixed-methods study of a tactile clay-making and AI system for personal reflection. It finds that AI can support meaning-making when its outputs remain provisional and negotiable, while users retain independent control through physical artefacts and selective engagement with AI representations.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of involving AI in reflection and emotional support without allowing AI to determine or override users’ interpretations of their own experiences. It investigates how generative AI can contribute to personal meaning-making while preserving user agency and interpretive authority.
AI.method: The authors developed ClayFlect, an MLLM-powered system combining tactile clay-making with conversational and visual generative AI. They conducted a mixed-methods study with 50 participants, examining how reflection progressed across physical artefacts, conversations, and AI-generated representations, and how participants accepted, modified, redirected, or rejected AI contributions.
AI.result: Reflection was distributed across material, conversational, and generated forms rather than being produced by AI interaction alone. Participants regarded AI outputs as provisional and selectively compared, reinterpreted, incorporated, redirected, or ignored them. Clay offered a directly manipulable space for independent meaning development, while AI-generated representations expanded possibilities that participants might not have been able to create or visualise themselves.
AI.conclusion: Generative AI can support personal reflection when its representations remain negotiable rather than authoritative. Systems should enable movement across multiple forms of representation, preserve parallel sites of user control, and allow AI involvement to recede or intensify according to the user’s evolving reflective process.

title: Supporting Allyship in Virtual Collaboration with Artificial Intelligence: A Scenario-Based Study
summary: Recent research has revealed that accessibility in virtual collaboration is not only a technical problem but also depends on allyship: the informal, interpersonal practices through which people support others' accessibility needs. Yet little research has examined how artificial intelligence (AI) might support allyship in collaborative accessibility contexts. To address this gap, we conducted a study where 18 participants (10 disabled, 8 non-disabled) reflected on four allyship scenarios with novel AI tools. Participants valued AI designs that they anticipated could help teammates express, interpret, and coordinate around access needs by reducing repeated disclosure and making allyship more actionable. At the same time, participants raised concerns when AI acted without consent, misrepresented users' intentions, or displaced the interpersonal work of allyship. Based on our findings, we introduce allyship-support tools as a class of accessibility technologies, offer design guidelines, and discuss AI in particular as a means of supporting allyship.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how AI can support accessibility allyship in virtual collaboration. Through a study with 18 participants, it identifies opportunities for AI to help people express, interpret, and coordinate around access needs, while emphasizing consent, accurate representation, and preservation of interpersonal responsibility.
AI.motivation: Existing accessibility research often treats virtual collaboration as a technical design problem, while accessibility also depends on allyship—the interpersonal practices through which collaborators recognize and respond to access needs. The paper addresses the limited understanding of how AI could support, rather than undermine, this form of allyship.
AI.method: The researchers conducted a qualitative study with 18 participants: 10 disabled and 8 non-disabled people. Participants reflected on four allyship scenarios involving novel AI tools. Their responses were analyzed to identify perceived benefits, risks, and design requirements for AI-supported accessibility allyship.
AI.result: Participants saw value in AI tools that could help teammates communicate access needs, interpret those needs, and coordinate supportive actions. They especially appreciated the potential to reduce repeated disclosure and make allyship more concrete and actionable. However, they were concerned about AI acting without consent, inaccurately representing users' intentions, and replacing the interpersonal labor and responsibility central to allyship.
AI.conclusion: The paper proposes allyship-support tools as a distinct class of accessibility technology and provides design guidelines for developing them. It argues that AI should augment interpersonal allyship—not automate it away—by prioritizing consent, user control, faithful representation, and collaborative coordination.

title: Move Fast and Mend Things: Keeping Up with Evolving AI Harms Using Social Media Commentary
summary: The rapid deployment of AI systems has created socio-technical, psychological, and operational harms that can elude ex-ante threat modelling and ex-post incident tracking. We introduce an LLM-assisted thematic analysis pipeline to dynamically detect, categorise, and track emerging AI harms from large-scale social media data. Applying it to 5.7 million Reddit post summaries over 18 months (01/2025 to 06/2026), we curate and release a dataset of 575,000 AI harm-related posts and a bottom-up AI harm taxonomy of 12 categories and 47 subnodes. The taxonomy reliably covers established expert-defined risks while surfacing granular harms that top-down frameworks overlook, such as distinct forms of AI privacy violations. Temporal analysis surfaces evolving user-centric harms, such as agentic privacy and security breaches, premature AI adoption in the workplace, and grief from AI companion discontinuation. Our pipeline shortens harm-detection timelines and hereby complements efforts towards more participatory and responsive AI governance.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an LLM-assisted pipeline that analyzes large-scale Reddit data to detect and track emerging AI-related harms. It produces a 575,000-post dataset and a bottom-up taxonomy of 12 categories and 47 subcategories, identifying both known risks and overlooked, evolving user-centric harms.
AI.motivation: Conventional AI risk assessment often relies on expert-defined frameworks and either anticipates harms before deployment or records incidents after they occur. These approaches can miss rapidly emerging, granular, and user-experienced harms. The paper aims to provide a scalable, dynamic, and participatory method for detecting and monitoring such harms from public discourse.
AI.method: The authors apply an LLM-assisted thematic analysis pipeline to summaries of 5.7 million Reddit posts collected over 18 months, from January 2025 through June 2026. The pipeline identifies AI-harm-related content, organizes it inductively into a bottom-up taxonomy, and performs temporal analysis to examine how harm patterns evolve. The resulting resource includes 575,000 AI harm-related posts, 12 high-level categories, and 47 subnodes.
AI.result: The taxonomy reportedly captures established expert-defined AI risks while also revealing more granular harms that top-down frameworks may overlook, including distinct types of AI privacy violations. Temporal analysis highlights emerging concerns such as privacy and security breaches involving AI agents, premature workplace AI adoption, and grief associated with the discontinuation of AI companions. The paper also claims that the pipeline reduces the time needed to detect emerging harms.
AI.conclusion: The study argues that LLM-assisted analysis of social media can complement traditional AI risk assessment by enabling faster, more fine-grained, and user-centered monitoring. Its dataset and taxonomy may support more participatory and responsive AI governance, although the abstract does not provide details on validation procedures, sampling bias, model reliability, or causal interpretation.

title: "Just Like This": Manner Deixis at the Graphics Interface
summary: People communicate how things should move by combining words with demonstrations: "open it like this." We present an interaction technique that brings this expressive resource to conversational 3D authoring. Building on "Put-That-There," our system combines speech, pointing, and spatiotemporal demonstrations to specify editable behavior. A hand movement supplies evidence for a mechanism's axis, pivot, range, and pace; an animated preview makes the interpretation inspectable. Users refine behavior through further words or demonstrations, and the system can request a demonstration to clarify intent. In a twelve-participant study comparing three input configurations, our system achieved 89% participant-declared completion versus 47% with speech alone, had the highest observed match rates on six categorical accuracy measures and tied on two, and was preferred by nine participants. This work makes demonstration part of an ongoing authoring conversation: behavior can be shown, inspected, and revised.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a multimodal conversational 3D authoring technique in which users combine speech, pointing, and spatiotemporal hand demonstrations to specify editable object behavior. In a 12-participant study, it substantially outperformed speech-only input in completion, accuracy, and user preference.
AI.motivation: Words alone are often insufficient for communicating how a 3D object should move, especially when intent involves spatial and temporal properties such as an axis, pivot, range, and pace. The paper is motivated by the need to incorporate demonstrations as an expressive, inspectable, and revisable part of conversational 3D authoring.
AI.method: The system extends the Put-That-There interaction paradigm by integrating speech, pointing, and hand-motion demonstrations. A demonstration provides evidence about a mechanism’s motion axis, pivot, range, and pace. The system generates an animated preview so users can inspect the inferred behavior, then refine it through additional language or demonstrations. It may also request a demonstration when the spoken instruction is ambiguous. The evaluation compared three input configurations in a 12-participant user study, measuring declared task completion, categorical behavior-matching accuracy, and user preference.
AI.result: The multimodal system achieved 89% participant-declared completion, compared with 47% for speech-only input. It obtained the highest observed match rates on six categorical accuracy measures and tied for the highest on two others. Nine of the twelve participants preferred the proposed system.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrations are effective as part of an ongoing authoring conversation rather than merely as a one-time input. Combining speech with spatial and temporal demonstrations enables users to show, inspect, and revise 3D behavior more successfully than speech alone, supporting expressive and interactive conversational authoring.

title: Drawing the Line: Where AI Guidance and Human Creativity Meet in Emotion-Driven Comic Storyboarding
comment: Copyright protected by IEEE, 10 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables, in proceedings of 14th International Conference on Affective Computing and Intelligent Interaction (ACII 2026)
summary: While generative AI models can produce visually faithful artwork, they often fall short in conveying emotional authenticity--a key driver of human expression. In visual storytelling, particularly comic storyboarding, this gap becomes pronounced: effective storyboards require both technical knowledge (e.g., anatomical accuracy or scenic composition) and emotional insight (from lived experience). We explore how human-AI collaboration can support emotion-driven creativity, where the user's feelings guide generation and emotional resonance is the goal. We present EmoToon, a technology probe that helps non-professional artists generate sketch-like storyboards and iterate on visual ideas. In a controlled study with N=25 participants, we find that AI assistance significantly improves emotional expression, aesthetic quality, and exploration, but reduces users' creative ownership. Our findings offer broader insights for human-AI co-creation in the domain of comic storytelling, emphasizing balance between output quality and user freedom, and raising new challenges for image generation models in this domain.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EmoToon, a human-AI co-creation tool for emotion-driven comic storyboarding. A controlled study with 25 participants shows that AI assistance improves emotional expression, aesthetic quality, and idea exploration, but decreases users’ sense of creative ownership.
AI.motivation: Generative AI can create visually convincing images but often struggles to convey emotionally authentic expression. This limitation is especially important in comic storyboarding, which requires both technical visual skills and emotional insight. The paper addresses how AI can support non-professional artists while allowing users’ feelings and intentions to remain central to the creative process.
AI.method: The authors developed EmoToon as a technology probe for generating sketch-like comic storyboards and supporting iterative visual ideation. They evaluated it in a controlled user study with N=25 participants, comparing creative outcomes and user experiences with AI assistance. The evaluation focused on emotional expression, aesthetic quality, exploration of ideas, and perceived creative ownership.
AI.result: AI assistance significantly improved participants’ emotional expression, aesthetic quality, and exploration of visual ideas. However, participants reported reduced creative ownership, indicating a trade-off: the system enhanced the quality and breadth of outputs while potentially weakening users’ sense of authorship and control.
AI.conclusion: Human-AI co-creation tools for comics should balance output quality with user freedom and authorship. EmoToon demonstrates the potential of emotion-guided generation for supporting non-professional creators, while also revealing challenges for image-generation systems in preserving emotional authenticity and creative ownership.

title: AI-Assisted Submissions in Online Research Are Rare and Highly Concentrated but Routinely Approved
summary: Online research platforms underpin much of what science claims about people, on the assumption that a human produced each response. Generative AI threatens that assumption by letting participants delegate responses to a chatbot, yet how often they do so remains unclear because prior estimates rely on self-report or automated detection rather than direct observation. We surveyed 2,500 workers on a high quality online research platform and directly observed AI assistance by linking donated ChatGPT histories to platform submission records of weekly ChatGPT users, covering 712,930 submissions across more than 127,000 studies. Although one in eight surveyed workers reported ever using AI on a study and 68% of observed workers had done so, assistance appeared in only 1% of submissions, with no detectable increase over more than 3 years. Assistance was often temporally localized within tasks and highly concentrated among workers, with 5% accounting for 64% of assisted submissions. Where assistance occurred, workers were virtually always paid, even when study instructions prohibited AI use, with overall approval rates similar to those for unassisted submissions. Half of assisted submissions involved bounded responses, outside the scope of the platform's LLM detector for open-ended responses. Taken together, our results do not support the view that AI assistance currently poses an existential threat to online research, but reveal limited payment consequences for prohibited use and gaps in platform safeguards, leaving platforms poorly prepared should that threat materialize.

AI.tldr: The paper directly measures chatbot assistance in online research participation and finds that it is widespread among some workers but rare at the submission level. AI assistance currently has limited observable impact on data quality and payment outcomes, while platform safeguards remain inadequate.
AI.motivation: The study addresses uncertainty about how frequently online research participants use generative AI to complete study tasks. Prior estimates relied on self-reports or automated detectors, which may be inaccurate or incomplete. The authors seek direct behavioral evidence by linking donated ChatGPT histories with actual platform submissions.
AI.method: The researchers surveyed 2,500 workers on a high-quality online research platform and linked donated ChatGPT usage histories to platform records for weekly ChatGPT users. The linked dataset covered 712,930 submissions across more than 127,000 studies. They compared AI-assisted and unassisted submissions with respect to frequency, timing, worker concentration, payment, approval, task type, and detectability by the platform’s LLM detector.
AI.result: One in eight surveyed workers reported ever using AI for a study, while 68% of observed workers had used AI. Nevertheless, AI assistance occurred in only 1% of submissions and showed no detectable growth over more than three years. Usage was concentrated: 5% of workers generated 64% of assisted submissions, and assistance often clustered within particular tasks. Workers were almost always paid for assisted submissions, including cases where AI use was prohibited, and approval rates were similar to those of unassisted submissions. Half of assisted submissions involved bounded responses that were outside the platform’s open-ended-response detector.
AI.conclusion: The findings do not indicate that AI assistance is currently an existential threat to online research validity. However, the mismatch between worker-level prevalence and submission-level frequency, the concentration of use, weak payment consequences for violations, and detector coverage gaps show that platforms are not well prepared for a possible future increase in AI-assisted participation.

title: Beyond Activation: Gaze Invocation with Visible Status for an Embodied AR Assistant in Co-Located Collaboration
summary: Wake words face an inherent trade-off: higher sensitivity reduces missed commands but increases accidental activations. In co-located augmented reality (AR), the system must also determine whether the user is speaking to the assistant or to a nearby person. We introduce a new perspective on this problem: combining gaze-based address with an embodied assistant, visible listening status, and turn management across activation, continued interaction, and release. In our implementation, users look at an assistant anchored in the scene and see activation progress and listening status on its body. Sustained gaze opens a local interaction channel; speech and playback keep it open when attention returns to the task; and inactivity closes it. We evaluated this design with 25 participants. After selecting the assistant's placement and dwell duration, each participant worked with a partner to plan a trip while using the assistant. The study recorded 500 interaction outcomes, including 496 assistant-directed utterance attempts. Gaze acquisition completed before speech for 490 of these attempts (98.8\%): 467 began while the channel remained open, whereas 23 began after it had been released. The other 6 attempts began before acquisition completed. Among 102 reviewed attempts in which gaze left after acquisition but before speech, the configured retention policy kept the channel open for 79 and released it before 23. The results show that an embodied target with visible status can support clear entry into an assistant interaction while revealing a different problem at release: after users look back to their work, they may not see that the assistant has stopped listening. We contribute the implemented gaze-invocation design and design implications for communicating assistant state after visual attention moves elsewhere.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a gaze-based, embodied wake-up and turn-management design for AR assistants that reduces ambiguity between assistant-directed and person-directed speech. In a 25-participant study, gaze reliably acquired the interaction channel before speech, but releasing the channel after users looked away was difficult for users to perceive.
AI.motivation: Traditional wake words require a sensitivity trade-off between missed commands and accidental activations. In co-located AR, the assistant must additionally distinguish speech addressed to it from speech addressed to nearby people. The paper therefore seeks a more explicit interaction mechanism that supports reliable activation, continued interaction, and release while making the assistant’s listening state understandable.
AI.method: The system uses an assistant embodied and anchored in the AR scene. Users direct sustained gaze toward it to open a local interaction channel, while activation progress and listening status are shown on the assistant’s body. Speech and audio playback maintain the channel when visual attention returns to the task, and inactivity closes it. The authors evaluated the design with 25 participants who selected the assistant’s placement and dwell duration, then worked with a partner on trip planning. The study recorded 500 interaction outcomes, including 496 assistant-directed utterance attempts, and reviewed cases involving gaze departure after acquisition.
AI.result: Gaze acquisition completed before speech in 490 of 496 assistant-directed attempts (98.8%). Of these, 467 utterances began while the channel was still open and 23 began after release; 6 began before acquisition completed. Among 102 reviewed cases where gaze left after acquisition but before speech, the retention policy kept the channel open in 79 cases and released it in 23. These findings indicate strong support for interaction entry but weaker user awareness of channel release after gaze shifts away.
AI.conclusion: An embodied AR assistant with visible activation and listening feedback can provide a clear alternative to wake words for initiating assistant-directed interaction. The main unresolved issue is post-attention state communication: users may not notice that listening has ended after they return their gaze to other work. Future designs should make release and current listening status perceivable without requiring users to keep looking at the assistant.

title: Many Brains, One Geometry: A Shared Visual-Semantic Space for Cross-Dataset fMRI Decoding
comment: 21 pages, 5 figures, 1 table, 3 supplementary figures, 2 supplementary tables
summary: Visual decoding from fMRI is typically siloed by participant and experiment, obscuring whether heterogeneous neural measurements can be organized within a common computational geometry. Here we introduce BRAID-fMRI (Brain Representation Alignment across Individuals and Datasets), a shared CLIP-supervised decoding framework. BRAID-fMRI uses a single ROI-wise Transformer with optional participant conditioning across eight visual-fMRI datasets comprising 93 dataset-specific participant entries, 430,007 single-trial responses and 162,839 unique stimuli. Regional brain activity is aligned with 512-dimensional CLIP ViT-B/32 representations using a multi-positive contrastive objective that treats repeated stimuli across participants and datasets as positives. BRAID-fMRI supports retrieval across seven evaluation datasets. On eight matched participant entries, it achieves 35.0 +/- 11.1% Top-10 accuracy, exceeding the observed mean accuracy of the two evaluated baselines - the MindEye-style pooled-CLIP decoder (27.1 +/- 5.1%) and ridge regression (21.1 +/- 9.1%) - and attaining the highest observed accuracy for seven of eight entries. In separately trained participant-agnostic models, expanding the source pool increased target-dataset holdout accuracy by up to 92.1% relative to the initial source-training condition. The learned space preserves graded semantic structure, while ablations and saliency highlight ventral and early visual cortex and category-specific motion and attentional systems. These results support scalable cross-dataset decoding into a common CLIP-aligned space, with model sensitivity concentrated in ventral and early visual inputs.

AI.tldr: BRAID-fMRI is a unified, CLIP-supervised fMRI decoding framework that aligns visual brain responses from multiple participants and datasets into a shared semantic representation space. Using a single ROI-wise Transformer and multi-positive contrastive learning, it outperforms pooled-CLIP and ridge baselines in cross-dataset image retrieval and benefits from larger source-data pools.
AI.motivation: Existing visual fMRI decoding methods are often trained separately for each participant and experiment, making it difficult to determine whether heterogeneous measurements share a common computational geometry and limiting cross-participant or cross-dataset generalization. The paper addresses the need for a scalable decoding framework that can align neural responses across datasets in a common, semantically meaningful space.
AI.method: The authors introduce BRAID-fMRI, which uses one ROI-wise Transformer with optional participant conditioning across eight visual-fMRI datasets. Regional fMRI activity is mapped to 512-dimensional CLIP ViT-B/32 image representations. A multi-positive contrastive objective treats repeated stimuli observed across participants and datasets as positive pairs. The framework is evaluated through image retrieval on seven datasets, with comparisons against a MindEye-style pooled-CLIP decoder and ridge regression. Additional participant-agnostic experiments test how expanding the source-data pool affects target-dataset holdout performance, while ablations and saliency analyses identify influential brain regions and systems.
AI.result: Across eight matched participant entries, BRAID-fMRI achieves 35.0 ± 11.1% Top-10 retrieval accuracy, compared with 27.1 ± 5.1% for the pooled-CLIP baseline and 21.1 ± 9.1% for ridge regression. It obtains the highest observed accuracy for seven of eight entries. In participant-agnostic models, increasing the source-data pool improves target-dataset holdout accuracy by as much as 92.1% relative to the initial source-training condition. The learned representations preserve graded semantic structure, and saliency results emphasize ventral and early visual cortex as well as category-related motion and attention systems.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest that visual fMRI responses from diverse participants and datasets can be aligned into a shared CLIP-compatible representation space. BRAID-fMRI enables scalable cross-dataset decoding and benefits from pooled training data, although its sensitivity is concentrated primarily in ventral and early visual regions and may depend on the quality and comparability of the source datasets.

title: TutorLoop: Regulating Student Learning Behaviors via Sensor-in-the-Loop Generative Feedback
summary: We present TutorLoop, a sensor-in-the-loop system that regulates student learning behaviors by delivering adaptive feedback based on real-time cognitive states. Unlike prior large language model (LLM) tutors that directly depend on scenario-specific content, TutorLoop operates on sensor-derived signals captured via webcams. Moreover, unlike direct cognitive-to-feedback mappings that are short-sighted, the system employs a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agent to optimize the feedback type across the entire learning process. Finally, another LLM tutor refines feedback into human-like, context-aware messages. We evaluate TutorLoop in a large-scale user study (N=187), where a model trained offline is directly applied to a new learning task without retraining. Results show that TutorLoop provides less frequent yet more effective interventions, improving attention, reducing workload, increasing engagement, and ultimately enhancing learning outcomes. These findings highlight the potential of closed-loop, sensor-driven feedback for scalable human-AI integrated systems to support learning.

AI.tldr: TutorLoop is a sensor-driven, closed-loop LLM tutoring system that uses webcam-derived cognitive-state signals and deep reinforcement learning to select when and how to intervene. In a study with 187 participants, it generalized to a new learning task without retraining and improved attention, workload, engagement, and learning outcomes through fewer but more effective interventions.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM tutors often rely heavily on scenario-specific content, while direct mappings from inferred cognitive states to feedback can be short-sighted and fail to optimize support over an entire learning session. The paper aims to develop a scalable, content-independent, closed-loop tutoring approach that adapts interventions to learners’ changing states and long-term learning trajectories.
AI.method: TutorLoop captures sensor-derived signals from webcams as proxies for real-time cognitive states. A deep reinforcement learning agent selects the feedback type with the goal of optimizing outcomes across the complete learning process rather than making isolated state-to-feedback decisions. A separate LLM then converts the selected intervention into human-like, context-aware feedback. The system is evaluated in a large-scale user study with N=187, using an offline-trained model deployed on a new learning task without retraining.
AI.result: Compared with the reported baseline or prior approaches, TutorLoop delivered interventions less frequently but with greater effectiveness. It improved learners’ attention, reduced perceived workload, increased engagement, and enhanced learning outcomes. The offline-trained policy also transferred to a new task without additional training.
AI.conclusion: The findings support sensor-driven, closed-loop feedback as a promising architecture for scalable human-AI learning systems. Combining cognitive-state sensing, long-horizon DRL-based intervention selection, and LLM-based message generation can produce more efficient and effective tutoring, although the abstract does not specify the baselines, effect sizes, or limitations.

title: Before Bringing It Up: When and How AI Companions Should Use Memor
comment: 17 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Zihan Guo and Roxy He contributed equally to this work and share first authorship
summary: Memory can sustain AI companionship, yet even accurate recollection can be inappropriate to use. Two rounds of formative interviews with 14 users (n = 6 exploratory, n = 8 memory-focused) motivate asking what a companion should consider before using past information. Eight themes inform Reconsider, a single-call procedure with five checks and four handling modes, evaluated on 80 scenarios across five models over 400 blinded within-model pairs. Two LLM judges favored Reconsider by net margins of +15 and +23 percentage points, with bootstrap intervals excluding zero for three of five models but not for GPT or Claude. Evaluator analysis linked judge scoring differences to model family, and a preliminary matched-guidance control isolating memory-specific content gave positive margins. We contribute an interview-grounded design framework for memory use and an evaluation that scrutinizes its own evaluators.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how AI companions should decide whether and how to use remembered user information. It develops Reconsider, a pre-use deliberation procedure, and evaluates it through interviews, scenario-based model comparisons, and judge-bias analysis. Results generally favor Reconsider, although effects are model-dependent and absent for GPT and Claude.
AI.motivation: Accurate memory is not always appropriate to deploy in an AI-companion interaction. The authors aim to identify the considerations that should guide memory use and to create a practical mechanism that helps models avoid insensitive, irrelevant, or otherwise inappropriate references to past information. They also address a methodological concern: evaluations of conversational quality may themselves vary across model families or contain evaluator bias.
AI.method: The study used two formative interview rounds with 14 users: 6 exploratory participants and 8 participants focused on memory use. Eight themes from these interviews were translated into Reconsider, a single-call procedure consisting of five checks and four possible handling modes. The procedure was evaluated on 80 scenarios using five language models, producing 400 blinded within-model pairwise comparisons. Two LLM judges assessed outputs, and the authors analyzed judge-score differences by model family. A preliminary matched-guidance control was also used to isolate the contribution of memory-specific guidance.
AI.result: Both LLM judges favored Reconsider, with net preference margins of 15 and 23 percentage points. Bootstrap intervals excluded zero for three of the five models, indicating statistically supported gains for those models, but not for GPT or Claude. The analysis found that evaluation differences were associated with model family. The matched-guidance control produced positive margins, suggesting that the benefit was not solely attributable to generic response-improvement instructions.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes an interview-grounded framework for deciding how AI companions should use memory and a practical Reconsider procedure for moderating memory use. Its evaluation supports the procedure overall but shows that effectiveness is model-dependent. By examining evaluator behavior and model-family effects, the paper argues that assessments of memory-aware interaction should scrutinize their own measurement process rather than treating judge preferences as universally reliable.

title: Human-AI Conversational Behaviors Predict Unassisted Task Performance
summary: Assistance from AI tools has supported and improved human performance across domains. However, recent research suggests that these immediate benefits may entail future costs, including diminished performance when AI assistance is no longer available. We study how human-AI interaction behaviors correlate with immediate and future unassisted task performance across two game-based problem-solving user studies ($n=139$ and $n=111$), using a \textit{dialogue act} framework adopted from a tutor-student dialogue taxonomy. In our studies, verbalizing thought processes correlates with higher unassisted outcomes, whereas directly requesting solutions correlates negatively. Similar to these participant-side patterns, assistant explanations of the current problem state are associated with better subsequent unassisted performance, whereas directly providing the next action is associated with worse performance. Qualitative and subtype analyses further show that ostensibly similar reasoning turns can elicit different assistance. Our findings suggest that preserving users' cognitive participation in problem-solving may support performance beyond AI-assisted interaction.

AI.tldr: The paper examines how different human–AI dialogue behaviors relate to immediate assisted performance and later performance without AI in game-based problem-solving tasks. Across two studies, maintaining active cognitive engagement—especially verbalizing one’s reasoning—is linked to better transfer, while requesting or receiving direct solutions is linked to poorer unassisted performance.
AI.motivation: Although AI assistance can improve performance during interaction, it may reduce people’s ability to solve problems independently afterward. The paper addresses this potential hidden cost by investigating which interaction behaviors preserve or undermine users’ cognitive participation and future unassisted performance.
AI.method: The authors conducted two game-based problem-solving user studies with 139 and 111 participants. They analyzed human–AI interactions using a dialogue-act framework adapted from tutor–student dialogue taxonomies, examining how participant behaviors and assistant responses correlated with immediate assisted outcomes and subsequent unassisted performance. Qualitative and subtype analyses were used to distinguish superficially similar reasoning turns that elicited different forms of assistance.
AI.result: Verbalizing thought processes was associated with better later unassisted performance, whereas directly requesting solutions was negatively associated with it. On the assistant side, explaining the current problem state predicted better subsequent independent performance, while directly supplying the next action predicted worse performance. The analyses also showed that similar-looking reasoning statements could trigger different kinds of assistance.
AI.conclusion: AI support is more likely to preserve future independent performance when it sustains users’ cognitive involvement rather than replacing their problem-solving decisions. Designing assistants to explain states and scaffold reasoning, instead of directly prescribing actions or solutions, may improve both immediate assistance and longer-term learning or transfer.

title: Structured pre-generation elicitation versus single-shot prompting in AI-assisted enterprise decision-making: a randomised online experiment
summary: Generative AI speeds, and mostly improves, professional work, but there is concern that users who delegate both the production and the evaluation of an answer may accept weak output and engage less with the underlying reasoning (cognitive surrender). Interventions proposed so far, such as unassisted practice or slowing adoption, sit outside the working task. We tested a different approach: an interactive metacognitive scaffolding layer (Cognistance, a prototype developed at the Oxford Centre for Impact Research (OCIR) that asks users to clarify context, choose a strategic direction and explain their reasoning before the AI generates a deliverable). Mean composite quality was 32% higher with the scaffold, with the same direction for every rater. Gains were largest for trade-off articulation and strategic coherence and absent for technical specificity. A large part of the aggregate effect reflected rescue of weak prompts: floor-scored (off-task) deliverables fell from 34% to 5%. Among participants whose own prompt already stated the data-localisation problem, the advantage was 21%. Treatment participants reported greater involvement and took about 2.4 minutes longer on average (10.46 minutes). Immediate recall scores were higher, which tentatively suggests better retention, but in this limited experiment, was not robust to sensitivity analyses. Self-ratings of quality did not track rated quality in either condition. Structured elicitation before generation improved the rated quality and task relevance of AI-assisted strategy documents at modest cost in time. Delayed retention, error detection and effects in live organisations are the priorities for the next stage of research.

AI.tldr: An interactive metacognitive scaffold added before AI generation substantially improved the rated quality and task relevance of strategy documents, mainly by preventing off-task outputs and strengthening trade-off articulation and strategic coherence. It required only a modest time increase, while evidence for improved retention remained inconclusive.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the risk of cognitive surrender in generative-AI-assisted work: when users outsource both production and evaluation, they may accept weak outputs and engage less with the reasoning behind them. Existing responses, such as unassisted practice or slowing AI adoption, occur outside the work task. The study therefore tests whether an in-task metacognitive intervention can preserve user engagement and improve deliverable quality.
AI.method: The study compared AI-assisted work with and without Cognistance, an interactive scaffolding layer developed by the Oxford Centre for Impact Research. Before generation, the scaffold required users to clarify the context, select a strategic direction, and explain their reasoning. Outcomes included rater-assessed composite quality, task relevance, trade-off articulation, strategic coherence, technical specificity, prompt quality, immediate recall, self-rated quality, involvement, and task completion time. The abstract also reports subgroup and sensitivity analyses.
AI.result: The scaffold increased mean composite quality by 32%, with improvements reported by every rater. The largest gains were in trade-off articulation and strategic coherence, while technical specificity did not improve. Off-task, floor-scored deliverables decreased from 34% to 5%, indicating that much of the overall effect came from rescuing weak prompts. Among participants whose prompts already identified the data-localisation problem, the advantage was 21%. Participants reported greater involvement and took approximately 2.4 additional minutes, completing the task in an average of 10.46 minutes. Immediate recall was higher, but this finding was not robust to sensitivity analyses. Self-assessed quality did not align with externally rated quality in either condition.
AI.conclusion: Structured elicitation before AI generation appears to improve the quality and relevance of AI-assisted strategy documents at a modest time cost, especially by preventing off-task responses and improving strategic reasoning. The findings support embedding metacognitive scaffolding directly into workflows rather than relying only on separate training or reduced AI use. However, the evidence for improved retention is tentative, and further research should examine delayed retention, error detection, generalisability to live organisational settings, and whether the benefits persist for users who already formulate strong prompts.

title: When My Skill Becomes Agent Skill: How Knowledge Workers Share Their Expertise with AI Systems
summary: Organizations have long sought to make workers' expertise reusable by others. Agentic AI changes the nature of such reuse by enabling AI systems to act on workers' knowledge with limited human involvement. This raises the question of how this shift shapes workers' willingness to share their expertise. We conducted an experiment with knowledge workers who created materials incorporating domain knowledge and decided whether to authorize human or AI reuse. We find that AI and human reuse differ primarily in whether workers choose to share their knowledge, rather than in what they choose to share. Participants' reasoning shifts from prosocial considerations when sharing with humans toward concerns about loss of control, replacement, and downstream governance when sharing with AI. These findings suggest that AI reuse may intensify tensions between organizational knowledge reuse and contributors' interests. We discuss implications for workplace AI and knowledge management policies that preserve workers' rights and agency.

AI.tldr: The paper examines how the possibility of AI reuse affects workers’ willingness to share expertise compared with human reuse. An experiment shows that AI primarily changes whether workers share, not the type of knowledge they share, and shifts their reasoning from prosocial motives to concerns about control, replacement, and governance.
AI.motivation: Organizations want workers’ expertise to be reusable, but agentic AI can act on that knowledge with limited human involvement. This creates uncertainty about whether workers will continue to share expertise when reuse may be mediated by AI and may reduce their control or agency.
AI.method: The authors conducted an experiment with knowledge workers. Participants created materials containing domain knowledge and then decided whether to authorize reuse by humans or by AI systems. The study compared sharing decisions and participants’ stated reasoning across the two reuse conditions.
AI.result: AI and human reuse differed mainly in workers’ willingness to share rather than in the content selected for sharing. Human reuse was associated with prosocial reasoning, whereas AI reuse prompted concerns about loss of control, possible replacement, and governance of downstream uses.
AI.conclusion: AI-mediated knowledge reuse may intensify conflicts between organizational goals for knowledge reuse and workers’ interests. Effective workplace AI and knowledge-management policies should protect contributors’ rights, control, and agency when their expertise is reused by AI systems.

title: Healthy skepticism in AI: a data visualization research agenda
summary: Research in data visualization of artificial intelligence (AI) models has historically focused on enhancing trust through visual explanations of AI. The trustworthiness line of work was built at least partially on an assumption that humans were critical users unlikely to adopt AI technology. It is increasingly clear that human trust levels in AI span, in fact, a wide range from critical to over-reliant. There is an urgent need to support both trust and healthy skepticism in AI solutions. We argue that it is healthy for humans to adopt a skeptical view both on the results of AI models and on the use of such AI models. We share our thoughts on the rising phenomenon of over-reliance on AI models, the risks and opportunities in using AI models, and the role of data visualization in over-reliance situations where humans are not motivated to engage in critical thinking.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that AI visualization should not only build trust but also promote calibrated trust and healthy skepticism, especially to counter human over-reliance on AI outputs.
AI.motivation: Prior AI visualization research has largely assumed that users are skeptical and need help trusting AI. The abstract highlights that users actually vary from critical to over-reliant, creating a need for approaches that support both appropriate trust and critical evaluation of AI systems and their outputs.
AI.method: This is a conceptual position and discussion paper. It synthesizes reflections on over-reliance on AI, the risks and opportunities of AI use, and how data visualization may influence human critical thinking when users are not motivated to scrutinize AI decisions.
AI.result: The paper identifies over-reliance as an emerging concern and argues that visual explanations intended to increase trust may be insufficient or potentially counterproductive for users who already trust AI excessively. It emphasizes visualization’s role in supporting skepticism and more critical engagement.
AI.conclusion: AI visualization should aim for calibrated trust rather than unconditional trust. Designs should help users question both AI results and the broader use of AI, particularly in situations where over-reliance reduces motivation to think critically.

title: AI-Driven Urge Regulation Assistant (AURA): Designing Preemptive Smart Wearables for Smoking Cessation
summary: Smoking cessation remains a complex self-regulatory challenge, often undermined by cue-triggered cravings arising from habitual, emotional, and social contexts. Existing wearable cessation systems are largely reactive, detecting smoking events only after lapses occur and thus missing the critical window for timely intervention. Guided by cue-reactivity theory and Self-Determination Theory (SDT), we argue that future digital health systems should shift from retrospective feedback toward proactive craving management that supports user autonomy and competence. To inform the design of such systems, we present a formative pilot qualitative study involving semi-structured interviews with 10 smokers and ex-smokers from a multi-ethnic Asian population, a demographic underrepresented in current wearable AI and smoking cessation research. Through an iterative co-design interview process, we examine (1) the barriers and facilitators to smoking cessation and (2) the desired design features of wearable systems targeting cravings before lapses occur. Our findings identify key craving predictors across habitual, emotional, and social dimensions, alongside user-preferred intervention strategies such as social accountability, personalized support, rewards, and just-in-time distraction techniques. Participants also emphasized the importance of trust, privacy, personalization, and non-judgmental interaction styles. These insights directly inform the design of AURA, a novel smartwatch-smartphone ecosystem for proactive craving detection and intervention using commercially available wearable devices.

AI.tldr: A formative qualitative co-design study explores how wearable systems can proactively detect and manage smoking cravings before lapses. Interviews with 10 smokers and ex-smokers identify craving triggers, preferred interventions, and trust-related design requirements, informing the AURA smartwatch–smartphone ecosystem.
AI.motivation: Current wearable smoking-cessation systems are mainly reactive: they detect smoking after a lapse rather than intervening during the earlier craving period. The study addresses this gap by investigating how systems can support proactive craving management, while also addressing the underrepresentation of multi-ethnic Asian populations in wearable AI and cessation research. Its theoretical motivation combines cue-reactivity theory with Self-Determination Theory, emphasizing timely support, autonomy, and competence.
AI.method: The authors conducted a formative pilot qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with 10 smokers and ex-smokers from a multi-ethnic Asian population. An iterative co-design interview process examined barriers and facilitators to cessation and elicited desired features for wearable systems that intervene before lapses. The findings were organized around habitual, emotional, and social craving predictors, as well as user preferences concerning intervention strategies and system qualities.
AI.result: Participants reported craving predictors spanning habitual routines, emotional states, and social contexts. Preferred interventions included social accountability, personalized support, rewards, and just-in-time distraction. They also stressed trust, privacy, personalization, and non-judgmental interaction. These findings were used to guide the design of AURA, a smartwatch–smartphone system intended to detect cravings proactively and deliver timely interventions using commercially available wearable devices.
AI.conclusion: The study argues that effective digital cessation systems should move beyond retrospective lapse detection toward proactive, autonomy-supportive craving management. Its qualitative design insights provide requirements for AURA and similar systems, particularly the need for personalized, privacy-conscious, trustworthy, and non-judgmental interventions that address multiple craving contexts. Because the study is a small formative pilot, its findings primarily support system design and hypothesis generation rather than broad effectiveness claims.

title: Empowering Users in Graph Rule Mining via Large Language Models
summary: In the era of interconnected data, graphs have emerged as an effective abstraction for modeling complex systems in an intuitive format, especially with the rise of Property Graphs, which offer an intuitive and scalable way of navigating non-intuitive structures. In this context, graph mining techniques have been developed for testing complex graph-based rules, as the MINE GRAPH RULE operator, which, however, require users to have prior expertise both in graph theory and formal query language. In this work, we propose to bridge the gap between users and the graph-association rule-mining process by showing how Large Language Models (LLMs) can be easily prompted to formulate, refine, and interpret complex relational rules, directly producing MINE GRAPH RULE queries.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using Large Language Models (LLMs) to help users formulate, refine, and interpret graph-association rules by generating MINE GRAPH RULE queries, reducing the need for specialized graph-theory and query-language expertise.
AI.motivation: Property Graphs are increasingly used to represent complex, interconnected systems, but graph-association rule mining remains difficult for non-expert users because operators such as MINE GRAPH RULE require knowledge of graph theory and formal query languages. The work aims to make this process more accessible through natural-language interaction with LLMs.
AI.method: The proposed approach prompts LLMs to translate user intentions into MINE GRAPH RULE queries and to support iterative rule refinement and interpretation. The abstract does not specify the prompting strategy, model evaluation protocol, datasets, baselines, or implementation details.
AI.result: The abstract claims that LLMs can be readily prompted to formulate, refine, and interpret complex relational rules and directly produce MINE GRAPH RULE queries. However, it reports no quantitative results, experimental comparisons, accuracy measures, or user-study findings.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are presented as an interface layer between users and graph-association rule mining, potentially lowering the technical barrier to querying Property Graphs. The strength of this conclusion cannot be fully assessed from the abstract because empirical evidence and evaluation details are not provided.

title: A Scoping Review and Experimental Study on Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback for Human-Robot Collaboration
summary: Human-Robot Collaboration (HRC) can facilitate mass customisation in Industry 4.0, with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) representing a promising approach for developing safe AI-based robots. Practical challenges remain regarding safety during AI development, human feedback quality, and bidirectional human-robot adaptation. We conducted a scoping review of RLHF in HRC systems, mapping methods that address these challenges. Following PRISMA guidelines, we screened 199 records and included 20 peer-reviewed publications (2020-2025) spanning multiple HRC domains. To our knowledge, this is the first review focused on the bidirectional, closed-loop design of RLHF. Our review found multiple feedback modalities enabling data collection in various feedback formats. Collected data can be integrated at different stages of AI training, resulting in a multi-step development process. Pilot experiments are commonly used to evaluate HRC systems based on both human and robot metrics. To empirically test a key gap identified in the review, we conducted a between-subjects VR experiment comparing system- and user-initiated feedback on robot proxemic behaviour for safe navigation. Using Bayesian models, we analysed the relation between the collected feedback and safety metrics: psychological safety (post-experiment questionnaire) and physical safety (inverse time-to-collision). Results show that user-initiated feedback captures perceived safety better than system-initiated feedback, indicating that feedback timing directly affects feedback quality. Our review and experiment findings show that RLHF relies on appropriate feedback methods to ensure AI safety in HRC, and future RLHF research should prioritise realistic HRC experiments evaluating the effects of feedback collection methods on relevant human and robot metrics.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a scoping review of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) in Human-Robot Collaboration (HRC), complemented by a virtual-reality experiment. It maps feedback methods, training integration points, and evaluation practices, then tests how feedback timing affects safety-related outcomes. The review covers 20 peer-reviewed studies, while the experiment finds that user-initiated feedback better captures perceived safety than system-initiated feedback.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by the need to develop safe, adaptable AI-based robots for mass customisation and Industry 4.0. Existing RLHF-in-HRC research faces three practical challenges: ensuring safety during AI development, obtaining high-quality human feedback, and enabling bidirectional adaptation between humans and robots. The authors identify a lack of systematic understanding of how feedback collection and timing influence the quality of safety-related learning signals, especially in closed-loop human-robot interaction.
AI.method: The authors conducted a PRISMA-guided scoping review of 199 records and included 20 peer-reviewed publications from 2020 to 2025 across multiple HRC domains. They categorised feedback modalities, data formats, points in the AI-training pipeline where feedback is integrated, and evaluation metrics. To investigate a gap identified by the review, they ran a between-subjects VR experiment comparing system-initiated and user-initiated feedback about robot proxemic behaviour during safe navigation. Bayesian models were used to analyse relationships between feedback and psychological safety, measured by a post-experiment questionnaire, and physical safety, measured using inverse time-to-collision.
AI.result: The review found that HRC-RLHF systems use diverse feedback modalities and formats, with feedback incorporated at multiple stages of a multi-step AI-development process. Pilot experiments commonly evaluate both human-centred and robot-centred metrics. In the VR experiment, user-initiated feedback was more effective than system-initiated feedback for capturing perceived psychological safety. The findings indicate that feedback timing influences feedback quality. The abstract does not report a clear advantage for either feedback condition on the physical-safety metric, inverse time-to-collision.
AI.conclusion: RLHF can support safer and more adaptive HRC, but its effectiveness depends substantially on how and when human feedback is collected. User-controlled feedback timing may provide a more valid measure of perceived safety than feedback requested by the system. Future research should use realistic HRC settings, examine feedback-collection effects experimentally, and jointly evaluate human outcomes and robot-performance or safety metrics.

title: Love for Believable AI: Artificial Partiality and Relationship Persistence as an Engineerable Stance
comment: 16 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Companion framework paper: arXiv:2607.15883 Code and data archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.21462976
summary: We study a behavioral mechanism for artificial partiality in conversational agents. The paper reports no human-subjects data and makes no claim about attachment, trust, perceived mind, or machine interiority. Partiality has two components: caring, defined as allocation of a finite interaction surplus above a guaranteed per-user service floor, and particularity, defined as a per-user state estimate accumulated from relationship history on fixed inference machinery. We implement both as a persistence layer over one open-weight base model and evaluate them on constructed multi-session relationships with known hidden-state schedules. A four-channel divergence compares known-user and stranger conditions on identical probes with paired generation seeds; the stranger prompt is not length-matched, and one channel (initiative) is an allocator output rather than generated behavior. The full mechanism reproduces the ordinal shape, but not the magnitude, of an analytically specified curve and is the only arm satisfying the protocol-defined joint signature on the calibrated battery. The initial mechanism fails probe-quality equivalence because relationship content reduces topical relevance. A guarded revision satisfies equivalence on the calibrated battery but not on a second battery not used in calibration, where it scores higher than the unmodified baseline. On that second battery, the specificity margin is 0.0198, below the 0.02 protocol threshold. The paired mean right-user--wrong-user estimation-accuracy contrast is 0.375 but is not positive in every run. The mechanism is therefore a candidate for a later perception study, not evidence that users perceive love. The versioned protocol record is not independently time-stamped and is not described as a preregistration. Ethical constraints include a stranger-treatment floor, a bounded surplus, disclosure, and de-intensification.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a computational mechanism for artificial partiality in conversational agents, separating caring (resource allocation above a service floor) from particularity (relationship-conditioned user-state estimation). It reports behavioral evidence under a constructed protocol, but does not test human perception or establish attachment, trust, love, or machine interiority. The evidence is promising but limited by calibration, battery generalization, protocol-registration limitations, and inconsistent run-level accuracy effects.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to operationalize artificial partiality without relying on claims about subjective experience or human responses. The paper aims to distinguish preferential allocation of interaction resources from relationship-specific inference, and to test whether these components produce a predefined behavioral signature under controlled known-user versus stranger comparisons.
AI.method: The authors implement caring and particularity as a persistence layer over one open-weight base model. They evaluate constructed multi-session relationships with known hidden-state schedules. A four-channel divergence metric compares known-user and stranger behavior on identical probes using paired generation seeds. However, the stranger prompt is not length-matched, and the initiative channel reflects allocator output rather than generated behavior. The study includes an initial mechanism, a guarded revision calibrated on one battery, and evaluation on a second battery. It also measures right-user versus wrong-user estimation accuracy and applies a protocol-defined joint-signature criterion.
AI.result: The full mechanism reproduces the ordinal form, but not the magnitude, of an analytically specified curve and is the only arm meeting the protocol-defined joint signature on the calibrated battery. The initial mechanism fails probe-quality equivalence because relationship content reduces topical relevance. The guarded revision passes equivalence on the calibrated battery but not on the second, non-calibration battery, where it performs above the unmodified baseline. Its specificity margin is 0.0198, below the 0.02 threshold. The paired mean right-user--wrong-user accuracy contrast is 0.375, but it is not positive in every run.
AI.conclusion: The mechanism should be regarded as a candidate for a future perception study rather than evidence that users perceive love or that the system has attachment or interiority. Interpretation is further constrained by prompt-length imbalance, the allocator-based initiative measure, limited generalization beyond the calibration battery, run-level inconsistency, and the absence of an independently time-stamped preregistration. The stated safeguards include a stranger-treatment floor, bounded surplus, disclosure, and de-intensification.

title: A Scale For Value Alignment In Human-AI Interaction
summary: Value alignment is a central objective in AI and HCI research, yet no validated instrument measures how users perceive it. This gap hampers the comparison and accumulation of findings and limits the effectiveness of applications, where understanding users' viewpoints is critical. We construct and evaluate a 13-item psychometric scale that measures perceived value alignment across two components: value understanding and value manifestation. It is based on a large item pool drawn from prior empirical studies, filtered by experts, and finally assessed by users (N=607) across diverse AI scenarios. Confirmatory factor analysis on an independent sample (N=259) confirmed the two-factor structure and high internal consistency for both subscales. Using optimization, we also derived a 6-item short form for quick administration. The scale is a reliable measure, providing HCI researchers with a common evaluation metric across contexts.

AI.tldr: The paper develops and validates a psychometric instrument for measuring users’ perceived value alignment with AI systems. The resulting scale has 13 items organized into two dimensions—value understanding and value manifestation—and a validated 6-item short form.
AI.motivation: Existing AI and HCI research lacks a validated, standardized measure of perceived value alignment. This makes it difficult to compare studies, accumulate evidence, and evaluate whether AI applications reflect users’ values from the users’ perspective.
AI.method: The authors generated a broad item pool from prior empirical research, refined it through expert screening, and evaluated the items with users across diverse AI scenarios (N=607). They then used confirmatory factor analysis on an independent sample (N=259) to test the factor structure and assess reliability. Optimization was used to derive a shorter 6-item version.
AI.result: The analysis supported a two-factor structure consisting of value understanding and value manifestation. Both subscales showed high internal consistency, and the 13-item scale was supported as a reliable measure. A 6-item short form was also developed for situations requiring rapid administration.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a validated and reusable metric for assessing perceived value alignment in AI and HCI. The full scale supports detailed evaluation, while the short form enables efficient measurement across applications and research contexts.

title: EEG and Eye-Tracking Evidence That AI Disclosure Shapes Face Evaluation
summary: AI-generated faces can be difficult to distinguish from real ones, leaving viewers to rely on source labels when judging an image. Yet prior work has made it difficult to separate the effects of what an image actually is from what viewers are told it is. We validated faces as AI-generated or human in an online study (N=169), then crossed actual source (AI, human) with label (none, Made with AI, Made by a human) in a lab study $N=30), recording event-related potentials (ERPs) and gaze. ERP responses were equivalent for AI-generated and real faces, but varied with the label: labels drew early attention (N2), while labels that conflicted with the face's actual source prompted re-evaluation of the face (P3). Affective processing and initial gaze orienting were unchanged, but labels altered visual exploration. We provide a validated stimulus set and evidence that attributed origin shapes face processing, with implications for disclosure design.

AI.tldr: The study shows that labels about whether a face was AI-generated or human influenced neural and visual processing more than the face’s actual origin. Labels attracted early attention, and mismatched labels triggered later re-evaluation, while emotional responses and initial gaze orientation were unchanged.
AI.motivation: AI-generated faces can appear highly realistic, making it difficult to determine whether viewers respond to the image itself or to information about its stated origin. The study addresses this gap by independently manipulating actual image source and source labels, enabling a direct test of how attribution affects face perception.
AI.method: The researchers first validated AI-generated and human-face stimuli in an online study with 169 participants. In a laboratory study with 30 participants, they crossed actual source (AI-generated versus human) with label condition (no label, “Made with AI,” or “Made by a human”). They recorded event-related potentials (ERPs) and eye movements to assess attention, evaluation, affective processing, and visual exploration.
AI.result: ERP responses did not differ reliably between AI-generated and human faces. In contrast, labels produced measurable effects: they elicited early attentional processing reflected in the N2 component, and source-incongruent labels led to later re-evaluation of the face, reflected in the P3 component. Labels did not alter affective processing or initial gaze orienting, but they changed subsequent visual exploration. The study also produced a validated stimulus set.
AI.conclusion: Perceived origin, communicated through labels, can shape face-processing mechanisms even when the visual stimulus itself is unchanged. The findings suggest that disclosure labels influence attention and interpretation rather than basic emotional responses or initial orienting, and they provide evidence relevant to the design of AI-content disclosures.

title: DuoSketch: How Pairs Navigate Challenges in AI-Supported Collaborative Design Ideation
summary: Generative AI offers new resources for collaborative design ideation, yet how designers work with it as a shared concept develops remains underexplored. We developed DuoSketch, integrating a shared canvas and live transcripts with a separate AI for each member of a pair. An exploratory qualitative study with 12 pairs identified three challenges: unresolved fit between AI proposals and shared design purposes, shared meanings not expressed in AI responses, and agreed changes missing from later outputs. We found that pairs navigated these challenges through bridging work in two directions: AI -> Shared Design (reworking features, developing uses, and assessing fit with shared requirements) and Shared Design -> AI (supplying materials, explaining meanings, and communicating decisions). We discuss how future AI systems can support the joint exploration and articulation of design ideas.

AI.tldr: The paper presents DuoSketch, a collaborative design system that gives each member of a pair a separate AI while maintaining a shared canvas and live transcript. A qualitative study of 12 pairs identifies challenges in aligning AI outputs with shared design goals and shows that designers perform bridging work between AI-generated suggestions and collectively developed ideas.
AI.motivation: Generative AI is increasingly used for design ideation, but its role in collaborative settings—where designers must establish shared meanings, coordinate decisions, and maintain a common design direction—remains insufficiently understood. The paper addresses this gap by examining how pairs work with AI while developing a shared concept.
AI.method: The authors developed DuoSketch, combining a shared canvas and live transcripts with a separate AI assistant for each member of a pair. They conducted an exploratory qualitative study involving 12 pairs and analyzed how participants interacted with the system and coordinated their design work.
AI.result: The study identified three central challenges: (1) AI proposals did not always fit the pair’s shared design purpose; (2) meanings shared by the designers were not adequately represented in AI responses; and (3) decisions agreed upon by the pair were not consistently reflected in subsequent AI outputs. Participants addressed these issues through two forms of bridging work: AI-to-Shared Design, involving reworking AI features, developing uses for suggestions, and evaluating fit with shared requirements; and Shared Design-to-AI, involving supplying relevant materials, explaining shared meanings, and communicating decisions.
AI.conclusion: Collaborative AI design tools should support continuous translation between AI outputs and the evolving shared design concept. In particular, future systems should help designers adapt AI suggestions, preserve shared context and decisions, and articulate tacit meanings and requirements to AI during joint ideation.

title: Active Inference for Interaction-Mediated Control of a High-Dimensional Robotic Arm
comment: 21 pages. 4 figures. To be published in the Springer CCIS series as part of the 7th International Workshop on Active Inference (IWAI26)
summary: We propose interaction-mediated control via Active Inference as a general architectural approach to high-dimensional control problems in Human--Computer Interaction (HCI). This architecture recasts user interaction as the provision of evidence about a latent task objective, rather than the direct specification of plant-control inputs. The mediating function is distributed between an interaction broker, which selects informative user queries and performs Bayesian inference over user preferences, and an Active Inference controller, which autonomously plans and acts under the resulting preference information to control the plant. This division of labour decouples the semantics of user interaction from those of low-level plant control. We instantiate the architecture in a simulated, multi-link robotic arm to perform a simultaneous whole-arm target-coverage task. A simulated user communicates exclusively through a clutch-style binary evaluative channel, without specifying joint-torque commands. Across increasing arm dimensionalities, the architecture achieves successful interaction-mediated control, although task success is lower than when the controller receives the true target preferences directly. Exact target-subset identification also remains imperfect, highlighting the distinction between preference inference and successful task completion. The experimental findings provide an initial computational demonstration of the proposed architecture under controlled, matched-model assumptions and motivate its further investigation in broader HCI applications.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and simulates an interaction-mediated control architecture that combines an interaction broker with an Active Inference controller. A user supplies binary evaluative feedback, which is used to infer latent preferences rather than direct control commands. In a simulated multi-link robotic arm, the architecture successfully performs whole-arm target coverage across increasing dimensionalities, but it underperforms direct access to true preferences and does not always identify the exact target subset.
AI.motivation: High-dimensional HCI control problems are difficult when users must directly specify low-level plant-control inputs. The paper is motivated by the need to separate the meaning of user interaction from the mechanics of autonomous control, allowing users to communicate task preferences while an intelligent controller plans and acts. It also addresses the challenge of inferring latent user objectives from sparse, indirect feedback.
AI.method: The authors design an interaction-mediated Active Inference architecture with two components: an interaction broker and an Active Inference controller. The broker selects informative queries and performs Bayesian inference over user preferences from a clutch-style binary evaluative channel. The controller uses the inferred preferences to plan and control a simulated multi-link robotic arm performing simultaneous whole-arm target coverage. Experiments vary arm dimensionality and compare inferred-preference control with a condition in which the controller receives the true target preferences directly, under matched-model simulation assumptions.
AI.result: The proposed architecture achieves successful interaction-mediated control as arm dimensionality increases, demonstrating that binary evaluative feedback can support effective task control without direct torque commands. However, performance is lower than in the true-preference condition. Exact identification of the target subset is imperfect, showing that accurate preference recovery is not necessary for successful task completion and that preference inference and behavioral success are distinct evaluation criteria.
AI.conclusion: The study provides an initial computational proof of concept for using Active Inference and an interaction broker to mediate high-dimensional HCI control. The results support the feasibility of decoupling user-level preference communication from low-level plant control, while also exposing limitations in preference identification and the restricted realism of controlled, matched-model simulations. Broader validation in more complex tasks, users, interfaces, and model-mismatch conditions is needed.

title: PalmSpace: Towards a Versatile On-Palm Interaction Space through Unified Touch Modeling
summary: As smart glasses and lightweight MR devices become increasingly practical, input remains a key challenge. The bare palm is an always-available, tactile, and proprioceptively accessible surface, but it has neither an explicit coordinate system nor embedded touch sensing. Prior on-palm systems typically expose isolated touch events, discrete regions, continuous trajectories, or task-specific gestures, limiting the palm's ability to support precise selection and gesture manipulation through a common input representation. We present PalmSpace, a wrist-worn infrared system that exposes mode-aware, body-referenced absolute input on the bare palm without per-user sensing calibration. At the interaction level, PalmSpace jointly represents contact occurrence, interaction mode, and palm-referenced absolute location; at the model level, it learns these coupled outputs through a shared real-time representation. In leave-one-participant-out evaluation with 17 participants, PalmSpace achieved 6.7 mm mean localization error, 98.9% contact detection accuracy, and 96.7% F1 for four-class interaction-state recognition. User studies further demonstrated absolute pointing and dragging, eyes-free digit input, and representative multi-finger controls including scrolling and pinch-based map manipulation. These results show that a morphologically variable bare palm can function as a transferable, mode-aware interaction surface.

AI.tldr: PalmSpace is a wrist-worn infrared sensing system that turns the bare palm into a calibrated-free, body-referenced input surface for precise selection, pointing, dragging, and multi-finger interaction in smart glasses and lightweight MR devices.
AI.motivation: Current on-palm interaction systems usually provide only isolated touch events, discrete areas, trajectories, or task-specific gestures.
