Because the bare palm lacks a visible coordinate system and built-in touch sensing, it is difficult to support precise and general-purpose interaction. PalmSpace addresses this gap by seeking a unified representation of contact, interaction mode, and absolute palm-relative position without requiring per-user calibration.
AI.method: PalmSpace uses a wrist-worn infrared sensing system and a shared real-time model to jointly estimate contact occurrence, interaction mode, and palm-referenced absolute location. The system is evaluated using leave-one-participant-out validation with 17 participants, including localization, contact detection, and four-class interaction-state recognition. Additional user studies test absolute pointing and dragging, eyes-free digit entry, scrolling, and pinch-based map manipulation.
AI.result: The system achieved 6.7 mm mean localization error, 98.9% contact detection accuracy, and 96.7% F1 for four-class interaction-state recognition. User studies demonstrated practical support for pointing, dragging, eyes-free digit input, scrolling, and pinch-based map control.
AI.conclusion: PalmSpace shows that the morphologically variable bare palm can serve as a transferable, mode-aware, and precise interaction surface for wearable AR/MR systems, without per-user sensing calibration.

title: How assigned AI use before class shapes active student engagement in class
summary: AI learning tools are rapidly entering classrooms, but evidence about whether they help students learn is mixed and rests mostly on test scores. Comparatively less research addresses whether the use of AI changes students' live learning behaviors in class. Here, we report the results of a preregistered field experiment with 759 MBA students enrolled in ten sections of a course, in which each student was randomly assigned two of ten class sessions to prepare for with a purpose-built voice-based AI discussion partner. After two uses of the AI discussion partner, students made about 31% more voluntary contributions in each later class session. Students who used the AI discussion partner more also reported greater comfort speaking up and greater perceived learning, but not greater focus or motivation. These findings suggest that repeated practice with a voice-based AI partner can meaningfully increase students' engagement in class discussion, enhancing a critical intermediate learning outcome.

AI.tldr: A preregistered field experiment with 759 MBA students found that using a voice-based AI discussion partner twice increased students’ voluntary classroom contributions by approximately 31% in subsequent sessions. Greater use was also associated with more comfort speaking and higher perceived learning, but not with greater focus or motivation.
AI.motivation: Although AI learning tools are increasingly used in education, evidence of their effectiveness is mixed and commonly relies on test scores. The study addresses a gap concerning whether AI can change students’ real-time classroom learning behaviors, particularly participation in discussion.
AI.method: The researchers conducted a preregistered field experiment involving 759 MBA students across ten course sections. Each student was randomly assigned two of ten class sessions to prepare for using a purpose-built, voice-based AI discussion partner. Subsequent voluntary classroom contributions and self-reported experiences were measured, including comfort speaking, perceived learning, focus, and motivation.
AI.result: After two uses of the AI discussion partner, students made about 31% more voluntary contributions in each later class session. Students who used the tool more frequently also reported greater comfort speaking up and greater perceived learning. No corresponding increase was found in focus or motivation.
AI.conclusion: Repeated practice with a voice-based AI discussion partner can substantially increase students’ engagement in live classroom discussions. The findings indicate that AI may improve an important intermediate learning outcome—active participation—even when it does not increase students’ reported focus or motivation.
